To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) Asthma in pregnancy is a significant public health problem with an increased risk of complications for both the mother and her baby.

(i) the prevalence of asthma in pregnancy is 12%, (ii) asthma is associated with increased risk of maternal complications, such as pre-eclampsia and preterm birth, (iii) the risk of maternal complications can be minimized with optimal asthma control, and (iv) asthma medications, including inhaled steroids, are not associated with adverse outcomes in mother or baby.
asthma during pregnancy is associated with increased risk of adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes.

the management of asthma during pregnancy.
the identification of maternal complications and the management of asthma in pregnancy.
the identification of maternal complications associated with asthma and the impact of these complications on pregnancy outcomes.

maternal asthma, when well controlled, does not appear to be associated with adverse perinatal outcomes, and that there does not appear to have been an increase in the prevalence of asthma in the offspring of women who had asthma during their pregnancy.
asthma is associated with a number of maternal and neonatal complications.
the risk of asthma during pregnancy is increased, but the risk of adverse maternal and fetal outcome is not increased.

the presence of maternal asthma during pregnancy increases the risk of maternal complications and adverse outcomes for the baby.

asthma is associated with an increased risk of adverse outcomes during pregnancy, such as preeclampsia, preterm delivery and small-for-gestational age babies, but that this risk is reduced by adequate asthma management.

asthma in pregnancy is associated with a higher risk of maternal complications, including preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, and caesarean section.
